nodes.label: Altitude disease
nodes.answer: Move to a lower altitude immediately if symptoms like headache, nausea, or dizziness occur. Hydrate, rest, and descend at least 500-1000 meters if conditions worsen.

nodes.label: Mountain routes
nodes.answer: Choose a route that matches the group’s fitness, experience, equipment, weather window, and daylight. Study the route in segments, identify hazards and escape options, and set a turnaround time before departing.

nodes.label: Route types
nodes.answer: Common route types include loops, out-and-back routes, point-to-point traverses, summit routes, ridge routes, valley routes, and via ferratas. Each has different navigation, escape, transport, and weather considerations.

nodes.label: Loop route
nodes.answer: A loop route starts and finishes at the same place but returns by a different path. It can be efficient, but poor weather or a navigation error may leave you far from the simplest retreat.

nodes.label: Out-and-back route
nodes.answer: An out-and-back route follows the same path in both directions. It makes retreat straightforward, but conditions can change between the ascent and descent, so reassess snow, ice, visibility, and daylight on the return.

nodes.label: Point-to-point route
nodes.answer: A point-to-point route starts and finishes in different places, so plan transport or a shuttle in advance. Identify escape routes carefully, because returning the way you came may not be practical.

nodes.label: Summit route
nodes.answer: Summit routes often involve greater elevation gain, exposure, and rapidly changing weather. Plan the descent as carefully as the ascent, and remember that reaching the top is only halfway.

nodes.label: Ridge route
nodes.answer: Ridge routes can offer excellent views but may be exposed to wind, lightning, poor visibility, and difficult escape. Check the forecast carefully and have a lower alternative if conditions deteriorate.

nodes.label: Valley route
nodes.answer: Valley routes are often gentler and provide easier retreat, but they can be affected by flooding, river crossings, mud, and heat. Check water levels and weather upstream before relying on a valley route.

nodes.label: Via ferrata
nodes.answer: A via ferrata uses fixed cables, ladders, and anchors, but still requires a harness, energy-absorbing lanyard, helmet, and appropriate training. Check the route grading, weather, and exit options before committing.

nodes.label: Route difficulty
nodes.answer: Route difficulty depends on distance, elevation gain, terrain, exposure, navigation demands, and technical sections—not only on length. Compare the route’s hardest section with your group’s experience and current conditions.

nodes.label: Easy route
nodes.answer: An easy route usually follows a clear, well-marked path with limited exposure and straightforward navigation. Even easy routes require suitable footwear, water, weather awareness, and a plan for delays.

nodes.label: Moderate route
nodes.answer: A moderate route may include steeper sections, uneven ground, longer distance, or basic navigation challenges. Carry a map, check the forecast, and allow extra time for rough terrain and rest stops.

nodes.label: Difficult route
nodes.answer: Difficult routes can include exposure, loose rock, pathless sections, scrambling, snow, or complex navigation. Do not attempt them without relevant experience, suitable equipment, a reliable forecast, and a clear retreat plan.

nodes.label: Scrambling route
nodes.answer: Scrambling involves using your hands for balance or movement on rock. Assess the descent as well as the ascent, avoid wet or icy rock, and consider a helmet where rockfall or exposure is possible.

nodes.label: Route planning
nodes.answer: Plan a route by recording the start and finish, distance, elevation gain, key checkpoints, hazards, escape routes, expected timings, and turnaround time. Check the weather and route conditions immediately before departure.

nodes.label: Route card
nodes.answer: A route card lists each leg with its start point, bearing, distance, estimated time, terrain description, and escape option. Share it with a trusted person and update it if you change the plan.

nodes.label: Route hazards
nodes.answer: Identify route-specific hazards such as cliffs, exposure, rockfall, loose terrain, river crossings, snow, ice, and avalanche terrain. Decide in advance which conditions would make you turn back or choose an alternative.

nodes.label: Escape route
nodes.answer: Identify real escape routes before you need them, including where they lead, how long they take, and whether they are safe in the current conditions. Do not assume every path or valley provides a practical exit.

nodes.label: Turnaround point
nodes.answer: Set a turnaround time or point before leaving, based on daylight, weather, descent time, and a safety margin. Turn around on schedule even if the objective is close.

nodes.label: Route conditions
nodes.answer: Check recent trip reports, official notices, webcams, and local sources for current route conditions. A route that was straightforward in summer may require different skills and equipment after snow, rain, or thaw.

nodes.label: Route markings
nodes.answer: Use route markings as confirmation, not as a substitute for navigation. Markings can be missing, damaged, snow-covered, or misleading, so keep checking the map, compass, and terrain.

nodes.label: Water crossings
nodes.answer: Assess water depth, speed, footing, and downstream hazards before crossing. If the water is fast, murky, above knee depth, or rising, find an alternative route or wait rather than crossing.

nodes.label: Route alternatives
nodes.answer: Choose a lower, shorter, or more sheltered alternative before setting out. A good Plan B should still be enjoyable, achievable in the forecast conditions, and have reliable navigation and escape options.

nodes.label: Route description
nodes.answer: A useful route description includes start and finish points, distance, elevation gain and loss, terrain type, navigation difficulty, water sources, hazards, best season, and escape options.

nodes.label: Example route node
nodes.answer: Use a consistent structure for each real route: name, region, start and finish, distance, elevation gain, difficulty, terrain, season, water sources, hazards, escape routes, and navigation requirements.
